text:
mike: Quick spike idea: create a regional uplink-aggregator service to consolidate Private control plane egress. Instead of dozens/hundreds of peerings or per-customer ENIs, customers see a few stable egress IPs per region.
priya: That's a big change. What are the core benefits you expect?
mike: Fewer peering attachments for us, less route churn for customers, reduced ENI/quota pressure, and simplified customer firewall rules. Also easier central NAT/inspection options.
chen: Main cons: extra hop in request path and a centralized component that could become a blast radius or bottleneck. Need to think auth, perf, and failure modes.
sam: We shouldn't break end-to-end guarantees. Propose two modes: passthrough (TCP/TLS SNI level proxying with no termination) and terminate+reoriginate (for when we need inspection or advanced routing). Both secured with mTLS and per-customer credentials.
laura: For terminate mode we need a strict threat model, auditability, and proof that we're not snooping customer payloads unnecessarily. Customers will ask for logs of which paths were observed.
arjun: Implementation sketch: aggregator runs in hardened regional clusters. For passthrough we TCP-proxy with SNI routing to customer-facing backend and maintain mutual TLS between client and endpoint. For terminate mode we present customer-facing certs (via customer-specific certs or delegated certs), validate client certs, then open a new TLS connection upstream with our operator identity.
priya: So aggregator supports both: preserve end-to-end mTLS for customers that require it, and offer terminate-mode for customers that allow inspection. Document this clearly in the onboarding contract.
mike: Rough configuration example: \n```\nregion: us-east-1\nmode: passthrough | terminate\negress_ips: [3.80.12.8, 3.80.12.9]\nnat_behavior: sticky | ephemeral\n```
chen: IP preservation question: customers that map source IPs to tenant records will break if we NAT. Could we offer a pinned NAT mapping per-customer or per-tenant pinned IP? That's stateful and scales poorly.
sam: Hybrid suggestion: default ephemeral NAT for bursts and sticky NAT for long-lived control-plane sessions. Track session affinity via 5-tuple and TTL; if a customer needs stable source IPs, reserve a small pool pinned to them (extra cost).
laura: Rollout path: start with passthrough-only mode, limited customers in one region. Put aggregator behind existing peering attachments with dual-route tables for canary. Observe p95 latency and connection churn.
arjun: Need a clear fallback: if aggregator goes unhealthy or overloads, route back to direct peering. That requires dynamic route updates or an operator-level fail-open route policy. Also backpressure semantics: when queueing grows beyond threshold, reject new sessions with explicit error code so caller can fallback.
chen: Operational concerns: NAT table exhaustion, conn-tracking memory, attack surface for connection storms. We'll need capacity model and autoscaling knobs.
priya: Security followups: (1) terminate-mode threat model and audit ingestion, (2) cert rotation per-customer and CRL/OCSP flows, (3) KMS/HSM use for private keys handling, (4) compliance notes for customers who require no-termination.
mike: Who wants to own work items?
laura: I'll take terminate-mode security review and cert rotation plan.
chen: I'll run numbers for NAT state capacity, conn-tracking scaling, and run a few failure-mode simulations.
sam: I'll draft fallback/backpressure contract, metrics to monitor (p95 egress latency, nat table utilization, connection churn rate, proxy CPU/memory per-tenant), and an SLO matrix.
arjun: I'll produce the migration playbook: pre-checks, dual-routing canary, cutover step, rollback paths, and post-cutover verification queries.
ops-bot: deploy-bot: branch created https://git.redwood.internal/uplink-aggregator/spike-2026, cluster aggregator-usw2-provisioned.
priya: We should also consider customer-facing controls: an opt-in flag for aggregator use and an explicit contract that lists mode (passthrough vs terminate), egress IPs, and expected latency impact.
mike: Agreed. Next steps: I'll draft an RFC with diagrams, cost/benefit table, and the canary checklist. Aim to keep spike minimal and prefer passthrough-only for the first run.
laura: +1. small, observable rollout first and document audit outputs.
chen: +1. I'll share simulated datasets for NAT scaling.
sam: +1. I'll prototype health signals for backpressure.
arjun: I'll prepare the operator runbook for emergency bypass.
priya: Great. Ping this thread when RFC link is up. :thumbsup:
